Sudha (25) has been on the billing team for three years. Since Harish, her former desk-mate, became team lead in April, the team's stand-ups have got shorter and quieter. I asked Sudha why.
She took a while. 'He doesn't come to our lunch table any more. Fine, he's busy. But when I raised the tax rounding issue in May, he said, "I've already decided that." So now I think twice. Three times. Mostly I don't say it.'
She told me, almost as an aside, that she had spotted a second rounding problem two weeks ago and kept it to herself. It surfaced yesterday in a customer complaint.
'I used to be the one who asked the annoying questions,' she said. 'I miss that version of me.'
Next step: speak to Harish about how the team is experiencing him, and set up an open issue list anyone can add to.

Coaching notes, session 4. Written by Maria, leadership coach.
Dilnaz (26) has led the design team at the agency for five months. I asked about the 360-degree feedback that came in last week.
She waved the printout. 'Two people said I don't listen. Honestly? One of them wanted this role. It's jealousy. The other one just doesn't have the vision for where we're going.'
I asked about the comment that her deadlines were unrealistic. 'Clients like ambition,' she said. 'People who can't keep up always call it unrealistic.'
When I asked whether any of the feedback might be useful, she smiled politely and moved on to her plans for a new logo system.
What I notice: every critical remark is explained by the other person's motive, never checked against what happened. Two projects have slipped this quarter.
Next session: I'll ask her to pick one piece of feedback and look only at the facts behind it.

The storm had knocked out power across half of Pune, and Francis sat in the office on the generator, staring at the delivery tracker. Red, all the way down.
Three weeks ago he'd switched the packaging supplier to save money. He hadn't asked the team. Ankita had mentioned, once, that the new supplier had missed deadlines for another client. He'd said, 'I've looked into it.' He hadn't, really.

On Monday morning in the Stockholm office, Selin asked the whole team to stay after stand-up. Coffee cups, rain on the windows, some people still in their coats.

Mentor's notebook. Written by Mohit.
Met Sudha for our monthly coffee today. She was promoted to operations lead two months ago, and she's doing well: costs down, the delivery backlog cleared.
But I noticed it in the quarterly review last week and again today. 'I cut the costs.' 'I fixed the backlog.' 'I renegotiated the courier deal.' Every win, I. At the review, two people from her team glanced at each other when she said it. I don't think she saw.
I know that glow. I had it too, the year I was promoted.
Today, walking back to the car, I said quietly, 'Can I tell you something as a friend? Your team is noticing the "I". The backlog was Neeraj and Shobha as much as you.'
She stopped. Her face went tight for a second. Then she said, 'Oh. Oh no. You're right.' She thanked me before she got in the car.

Aadhya called tonight, happy, to tell me about the client presentation. It went well. I'm glad. But I counted, somewhere in the middle: 'my strategy', 'my deck', 'I closed it', 'I told them'. Maybe fourteen times. Her team of five did most of that deck. I know, because Leena was up till two on it and texted me.
Two months ago Aadhya was the person who always said 'we'. The promotion's changed something.

So at the end of the call I said, 'Can I say one small thing, as your friend? Your team might be hearing a lot of "I" lately.'

I'm Devika, Wasim's cousin. I stayed with his family for the summer, so I can only say what I saw.
Wasim failed his Class 10 maths in May. His parents were fighting a lot then, doors banging. He spent most days in his room.
In June he started going to something he called 'the youth circle', in a rented hall near the bus depot. Two older boys came on a motorbike to pick him up. They brought him back late, with samosas for everyone, and called my aunt 'Aunty-ji' very politely.
